result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.steiner_tree()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find an approximate Steiner tree connecting the given terminal nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L23259-L23395){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.steiner_tree( terminal_nodes, weight_attr=None, return_subgraph=True, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Steiner tree](/assets/graphs/algo-steiner-tree.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A seven-node graph with three terminal nodes labeled t1, t2, and t3 in the accent color. A Steiner tree drawn in the accent color connects all three terminals by passing through two smaller non-terminal Steiner nodes. Two additional non-tree edges on the perimeter show alternative routes that the Steiner tree avoids." width="100%"} A Steiner tree is a minimum weight tree that connects a specified set of terminal nodes. It may include additional non-terminal nodes (called Steiner nodes) if they help reduce the total weight. This implementation uses Mehlhorn's algorithm which provides a 2-approximation. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [terminal_nodes]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of node labels that must be connected by the tree. Must contain at least 2 nodes. [weight_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of edge attribute to use for weights. If `None` (default), uses the edge's weight field. If the attribute doesn't exist on an edge, defaults to `1.0`. [return_subgraph]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns a new Graph containing only the Steiner tree edges. If `False`, returns a list of (source_label, target_label, weight) tuples. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph or list[tuple[str, str, float]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Either a new Graph with Steiner tree edges or a list of edge tuples, depending on the `return_subgraph=` parameter. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If fewer than 2 terminal nodes are provided, if any terminal node doesn't exist in the graph, or if the terminal nodes are not all connected. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The Steiner tree problem, finding the cheapest tree that spans a designated set of *terminal* nodes and may route through non-terminal "Steiner" nodes, is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard even on planar graphs. This implementation uses Mehlhorn's (1988) 2-approximation, which builds a metric closure of the terminals using shortest paths, takes an MST of that closure, and expands the tree edges back to their underlying subgraph paths, running in $O(|T| \cdot (E + V) \log V)$ time. The result is guaranteed to weigh no more than twice the true optimum; that ratio is tight in the worst case but is usually much better on structured inputs. Two-terminal inputs degenerate to a shortest path between the pair. ## Examples {.doc-examples} **Network Design: Connecting Data Centers** The three data centers aren't directly connected to each other, but they can all be joined through a shared backbone of routers; the Steiner tree finds the cheapest such connection, using routers as intermediate "Steiner nodes" where helpful: ::: {#21b0a10f .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(weighted=True) for node in ["DC1", "DC2", "DC3", "Router1", "Router2", "Router3"]: g.add_node(node) g.add_edge("DC1", "Router1", weight=10.0) g.add_edge("DC2", "Router1", weight=15.0) g.add_edge("DC3", "Router2", weight=12.0) g.add_edge("Router1", "Router2", weight=5.0) g.add_edge("Router2", "Router3", weight=8.0) g.add_edge("Router1", "Router3", weight=20.0) terminals = ["DC1", "DC2", "DC3"] steiner = g.steiner_tree(terminals) # Returns the number of edges needed to connect all three data centers steiner.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 4 ``` ::: ::: **Phylogenetics: Connecting Key Species** The same idea applies to evolutionary trees: connecting just the primates pulls in their shared common ancestor as a Steiner node, while leaving the more distantly related mouse out of the tree entirely: ::: {#6866401b .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(weighted=True) species = ["Human", "Chimp", "Gorilla", "Mouse", "CommonAncestor1", "CommonAncestor2"] for s in species: g.add_node(s) g.add_edge("Human", "CommonAncestor1", weight=1.0) g.add_edge("Chimp", "CommonAncestor1", weight=1.2) g.add_edge("CommonAncestor1", "CommonAncestor2", weight=3.0) g.add_edge("Gorilla", "CommonAncestor2", weight=2.5) g.add_edge("Mouse", "CommonAncestor2", weight=10.0) primates = ["Human", "Chimp", "Gorilla"] tree = g.steiner_tree(primates) # Returns the number of edges connecting the primates and their shared ancestors tree.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 4 ``` ::: :::
